newsitem.title: USA: Board votes to shut Conn. Yankee nuclear plant.
newsitem.headline: Board votes to shut Conn. Yankee nuclear plant.

text.p: Northeast Utilities said Wednesday the board of directors of the Connecticut Yankee nuclear power plant voted to retire the Haddam Neck, Conn. station.

"The low cost of replacement power, combined with the relative small size and age of Connecticut Yankee, make it in our customers' best interest to permanently retire the unit," Bruce Kenyon, president and chief executive officer of NU Nuclear, said in a statement.
The decision came after a special meeting of Connecticut Yankee's board to decide the fate of the 28-year-old plant, one of the nation's oldest nuclear facilities.

The board, citing an analysis showing poor economics for the plant amid high operating costs and growing competition from cheaper sources of power, said in October it was unlikely it would ever reopen.
The 582-megawatt (MW) Connecticut Yankee station had been shut down for repairs and refueling since July 22.
Northeast Utilities (NU), Connecticut Yankee's operator, owns 49 percent of the plant.
The balance is held by seven other New England utilities.

The other owners are New England Power Co, with a 15 percent stake; United Illuminating Co (9.5 percent); Boston Edison Co (9.5); Central Maine Power Co (6.0); Montaup Electric Co (4.5); Cambridge Electric Light Co (4.5); and Central Vermont Public Service Corp (2.0).
Each of Connecticut Yankee's owners will make arrangements to replace the electrical generation lost by permanently shutting down the plant, NU said in a statement.
Connecticut Yankee will now file its intention to decommission the plant with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC), and then has five years to file a decommissioning plan with the NRC.
Staffing at the plant is expected to be cut to just over 100 employees by the end of 1997, NU said.
Connecticut Yankee was the world leader in nuclear generation between 1980 and 1984.
Kenyon said NU will help set up a citizens' advisory board to ensure public involvement in the decommissioning process.
NU's beleaguered nuclear operation also includes its three Millstone stations in Waterford, Conn., which have been shut since March 31 due to various safety concerns.
The Millstone plants generated 2,670 MW of power.
The utility is being investigated by the NRC, which is meeting with NU officials Wednesday and Thursday to discuss why more than 100 violations of safety rules occurred over the past two years.
NU has emphasized in recent months that it is taking steps to shore up its nuclear operations, including a shakeup in top management.
Kenyon, who joined NU in September, said Tuesday the utility's past problems were caused by "leadership's pervasive tolerance of low standards."
But he said that since NU's reorganization, "we've changed the leadership, and we will no longer tolerate low standards."
Despite the decision to close Connecticut Yankee permanently, NU is still responsible for penalties and fines the plant has accumulated.

Connecticut Yankee was licensed to operate until 2007. But after its shutdown in July, an economic analysis showed that customers could potentially save $100 million or more by the early closing of the plant.
An NU spokesman said last month he was "cautiously optimistic" that NU would have enough power to meet demand this winter, even with its nuclear wing out of commission.
The utility will import up to 2,100 MW to meet the anticipated peak demand of 5,300 MW, the spokesman said.

Connecticut Yankee's board also on Wednesday authorized the redemption of $58 million of Connecticut Yankee's Series A first mortgage bonds, pursuant to the optional redemption provisions of the company's indenture. The redemption price is 102.4 percent of the principal amount, plus accrued interest, and the redemption date is January 8, 1997.
